newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup - Glints and Grins.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Closeup - Glints and Grins.

text.p: By Jim Middleton (ABC TV political correspondent)

Geoff Prosser gave the Opposition plenty to smile about this week, but as parliament wraps up for the winter there was a glint in some government eyes too. The prize for the man with the biggest grin in Canberra goes to Parliamentary Secretary Nick Minchin.

For a thin man he had a very broad smile indeed after the Opposition and the Democrats had rejected -- for a second time -- the government's plans for a voluntary vote on the constitutional convention, thereby consigning it almost certainly to the dustbin of history.

John Howard, the constitutional conservative, inherited the convention from Alexander Downer who'd come up with the idea as a way of avoiding having to deal with the split in coalition ranks over the republic. Howard doesn't want constitutional change, but kept the convention pledge as a way of neutralising the issue up in the run-up to the election.

He then handed carriage of the convention to Senator Minchin, one of the canniest political thinkers in the government's ranks, who came up with the proposal for a voluntary postal vote for half the delegates.
Howard provided an insight into his thoughts about the convention on his VIP plane on the way back from his trip to Singapore and China earlier this year.

Asked whether the convention's credibility would suffer if there were a small response to the ballot. His answer: To shrug and smile broadly. The implicit message: That would suit him just fine, because he thinks the current constitutional arrangements work just fine.

But neither Howard nor Minchin could have thought the Opposition and the Democrats would swallow their bait so deeply. By going to the wall over the voting arrangements the non-government parties may well have ensured the republic is off the agenda for the next election.

And that's not the only example of the government's tactics doing the trick during the week. Threats of double dissolution elections over a number of pieces of contentious legislation both called the Senate's bluff and split the Opposition parties.

For instance, the Democrats caved in and supported Judi Moylan's contentious legislation to reform the nursing home sector after the minister offered a $40 million dollar sweetener. This is the measure introducing up-front fees for nursing home entrants to provide the industry with the capital to upgrade facilities. Labor believes the fact that many entrants will have to sell their one major asset -- the family home -- to pay the euphemistically titled accommodation bond provides it with a potent election campaign weapon.
The democrats were convinced otherwise in negotiations masterminded by Moylan's astute adviser Jim Barron, aided and abetted by lobbyists for church-run nursing homes.
It will still be easy for Labor to run a scare campaign. The fact that the Democrats backed off on such a contentious subject signals just how uninterested they are in a double dissolution election.

Then there's work for the dole. It s a very popular idea with the punters -- this week, for instance, it was the most discussed subject on talkback radio around the nation. It's also split the Labor party. Kim Beazley wanted to let it slip through, the left had other ideas. In the Senate last Friday, John Faulkner declared Labor would reject the work for the dole bill, much to the government's pleasure.

"The lesson is: Never let the Senate sit by itself," was the cynical comment of one Labor hardhead. The government promptly announced rejection would provide another double dissolution trigger and Labor belatedly caved in. The effect is to diminish Labor's credibility on the subject. It also sparked a sharp spat in the ALP caucus over what Labor stood for these days.,

That had Peter Costello smiling in parliament on Tuesday -- a look which had been notably absent in the coalition party room earlier in the day when he put on his stern face to take Peter Reith to task over his suggestion of a plebiscite on GST.

Costello is all too aware of the difficulties of promoting tax reform and thought Reith had undermined his efforts. The Treasurer is doing his best not to frighten the horses. The signals so far point to a tax simply to replace most wholesale sales tax and ensnare services. The chief goal at the moment appears to be to bring it in under 10 percent. The aim is to sell any new tax as a necessary reform but without providing Labor with a Fightback!-style target during the election campaign.
Still a very big ask. But if Costello and Howard can pull it off their smiles will be broader and longer than any of the transitory pleasure Geoff Prosser's travails are giving Labor this week.
